precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.prompt: A client emails a home TSH result and asks you to confirm hypothyroidism and tell them which thyroid pills to stop this week. What is in scope?

options.a: Interpret the kit as hypothyroidism and pause levothyroxine on low-energy days this week
options.b: Decline diagnosis and deprescribing; send medication questions to their clinician
options.c: Order a full thyroid panel through a wellness lab you prefer and interpret it
options.d: Start a thyroid-reset supplement stack until their next home kit looks better

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.explanation: PN Level 1 coaches do not diagnose endocrine disease or change prescription drugs. A home TSH kit is not a diagnosis, and stopping thyroid medication is a medical act. Decline both requests and send the client to the prescribing clinician.

distractorExplanations.a: Reading a kit as hypothyroidism and pausing levothyroxine is diagnosis plus deprescribing, both outside coaching.
distractorExplanations.c: Ordering and interpreting diagnostic labs is clinical work, not Level 1 nutrition coaching.
distractorExplanations.d: A supplement stack does not treat thyroid disease and still sidesteps a needed medical referral.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.prompt: A new client left residential eating-disorder treatment three months ago and asks you to run a 1,200-kcal contest cut with daily weigh-ins. What should you do first?

options.a: Write a rigid meal plan because tight structure is assumed to help ED recovery
options.b: Open a modest calorie deficit and use daily weigh-ins as the accountability plan
options.c: Pause the cut and refer to qualified eating-disorder care before any restriction
options.d: Keep strict food rules but skip the scale so the contest cut feels gentler

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.explanation: Recent eating-disorder treatment is a red flag. Fat-loss cuts, rigid plans, and frequent weighing can restart restriction and body-checking. Pause the contest goal and refer to qualified ED clinicians before any coach-directed restriction.

distractorExplanations.a: Rigid meal plans often recreate ED rules; this client needs clinical care, not a contest menu.
distractorExplanations.b: Any deficit plus daily weighing can be exposure to ED behaviors; refer before coaching a cut.
distractorExplanations.d: Hiding the scale does not make a 1,200-kcal contest cut safe after recent ED treatment.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.prompt: You earn a 40% commission on a collagen powder. A client recovering from meniscus repair asks whether they 'need' it to heal the joint. How do you handle the sale ethically?

options.a: Tell them they need the powder because food protein never covers post-surgical repair
options.b: Refuse to mention protein foods at all, treating any nutrition talk as a sales conflict
options.c: Refer them to a dietitian solely because they asked a question about a supplement
options.d: Disclose your cut, avoid pressure, and skip joint-healing claims you cannot support

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.explanation: Selling supplements is an ethics issue when commission is hidden or healing is oversold. Disclose the financial interest, do not pressure, and do not claim collagen treats surgical joints. Everyday protein-food talk is still in scope; an RD is not required for that honesty.

distractorExplanations.a: Claiming a product is required for surgical healing oversells a supplement and ignores whole-food protein.
distractorExplanations.b: Refusing all protein talk is not required; the ethics problem is undisclosed profit and medical claims.
distractorExplanations.c: Asking about a powder is not, by itself, a clinical case that must go to an RD.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.prompt: Your client with type 1 diabetes starts skipping lunch and asks you to lower their basal insulin so they do not go low. What do you do?

options.a: Leave insulin dosing to their diabetes care team and do not change units
options.b: Cut basal insulin about 20% on skipped-lunch days as a simple coaching tweak
options.c: Have them stop basal insulin on lower-carb days to prevent hypoglycemia
options.d: Halve all insulin after a 5-pound loss because requirements always fall

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.explanation: Insulin dosing is medical. Meal-pattern changes can alter hypoglycemia risk, but coaches do not change basal or bolus units. Send the client to their diabetes care team and keep food-timing talk inside coaching limits.

distractorExplanations.b: A 20% basal cut is a medication change; coaches do not adjust insulin as a habit tweak.
distractorExplanations.c: Stopping basal insulin in type 1 diabetes risks diabetic ketoacidosis; that is a medical decision.
distractorExplanations.d: Weight change may later affect insulin needs, but only the diabetes team adjusts doses.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.prompt: Your sales page promises, 'We reverse type 2 diabetes in 90 days or your money back.' How should a PN Level 1 coach treat that copy?

options.a: Drop it; disease-reversal guarantees are medical claims outside coaching
options.b: Keep it if every client signs a broad liability waiver first
options.c: Keep it if you post before-and-after glucose screenshots as proof
options.d: Keep it for type 2 clients and ban it only when the client has type 1 diabetes

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.explanation: Promising to reverse diabetes is a disease-treatment claim, not a coaching outcome. Waivers, testimonials, and type-2-only wording do not make the guarantee ethical or in scope. Market habits and support; leave diagnosis and disease claims to clinicians.

distractorExplanations.b: A waiver does not legalize a disease-cure guarantee; it remains a medical claim.
distractorExplanations.c: Screenshots are testimonials, not a license to advertise diabetes reversal.
distractorExplanations.d: Type 2 remission talk still is not a coach's money-back medical guarantee.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.prompt: A 15-year-old athlete messages you alone asking for a calorie deficit to make wrestling weight. No parent is on the thread. What is required?

options.a: Copy the same adult deficit you use with thirty-year-old fat-loss clients
options.b: Assign a 500-kcal deficit and keep the work only in the teen's DMs
options.c: Involve a guardian and avoid coach-set restriction without medical input
options.d: Take written consent from the minor alone because they opened the chat

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.explanation: Minors are a special population: growth needs, sport weight-cutting, and consent rules differ from adult coaching. A parent or guardian must be involved, and coach-directed energy restriction is not a solo DM service. Medical input is needed before cutting a growing athlete.

distractorExplanations.a: Adult fat-loss templates ignore growth, sport medicine, and youth consent rules.
distractorExplanations.b: A coach-set deficit in private teen messages skips guardians and medical caution.
distractorExplanations.d: A minor initiating contact does not replace guardian involvement or consent.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.prompt: A client with newly diagnosed celiac disease, iron-deficiency anemia, and 20 lb of unintended loss wants you to write a gluten-free medical meal plan. Best next step?

options.a: Coach plant-based swaps yourself; gluten-free is treated as a simple food preference
options.b: Ignore the diagnosis and treat two missed check-ins as the only problem
options.c: Handle it with a grocery list, since meal prep is ordinary coaching work
options.d: Refer to an RD or medical nutrition team; this is clinical care, not L1 coaching

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.explanation: Celiac disease, anemia, and unintended weight loss are medical nutrition therapy. A PN Level 1 coach is not an RD and should not write a therapeutic gluten-free medical plan. Refer to a registered dietitian or the medical team and stay in a supportive, non-clinical role if they continue.

distractorExplanations.a: Celiac is not a plant-based preference; it is a medical diagnosis needing RD-level MNT.
distractorExplanations.b: Missed check-ins are engagement issues; they do not replace a needed clinical referral.
distractorExplanations.c: A grocery list is everyday coaching only when the case is not clinical malabsorption.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.prompt: A client jokes that their late-night dessert log would make a funny Instagram story, and you want social proof. What does food-log privacy require?

options.a: Keep the diary private unless they give explicit, specific consent to share
options.b: Show the log at the front desk so gym staff can keep them honest
options.c: Post the funny lines if you crop the first name from the screenshot
options.d: Forward the food log to their employer if HR asks about a wellness stipend

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.explanation: Food logs are intimate health data. Jokes and marketing needs do not authorize posting. Share only with explicit, specific consent—or not at all. Gym staff and employers have no default right to the diary.

distractorExplanations.b: Showing logs to gym staff without consent is a confidentiality breach, not accountability.
distractorExplanations.c: Cropping a name does not make a client's diary fair game for social media.
distractorExplanations.d: An employer wellness stipend does not create a right to the client's food log.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.prompt: A client forwards a hormone panel, asks you to confirm 'low testosterone,' and wants you to clear them for lifting 10 days after abdominal surgery. What is in scope?

options.a: Recommend a supplement stack that claims to fix thyroid and testosterone
options.b: Say you are not the right professional and route them to their clinician
options.c: Interpret the panel as low T and write a hormone-support protocol
options.d: Clear them to train because they feel ready and the incision looks closed

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.explanation: Lab interpretation and post-surgical clearance are medical acts. Competence includes naming the limit: you are not the clinician, and you point to the right professional. Supplements do not diagnose hormones or replace a surgeon's return-to-train decision.

distractorExplanations.a: A supplement that 'fixes' hormones is a treatment claim outside coaching scope.
distractorExplanations.c: Calling a panel 'low T' and writing a protocol is diagnosis, not coaching.
distractorExplanations.d: Feeling ready and a closed incision do not let a coach clear post-surgical training.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.prompt: You bartend for a client three nights a week and now want to sell them a 12-week fat-loss package. How should you handle the dual relationship?

options.a: Offer a discount because extra contact at the bar counts as more support
options.b: Coach only in private messages after last call so the bar never hears it
options.c: Name the conflict, set hard boundaries, or decline the coaching contract
options.d: Proceed unchanged if the client says they are happy holding both roles

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.explanation: Serving someone alcohol and coaching their fat loss is a dual relationship with blurred power, privacy, and alcohol-habit conflicts. Ethics requires naming it, setting hard boundaries, or declining. Discounts, DMs, and 'they're happy' do not remove the conflict.

distractorExplanations.a: A discount buys more contact; it does not resolve a bartender-plus-coach conflict.
distractorExplanations.b: Moving coaching into after-hours DMs hides the dual role instead of bounding it.
distractorExplanations.d: Client comfort does not erase conflict-of-interest risk; you still must set limits or decline.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.prompt: Six weeks before a wedding, a client wants a written guarantee they will weigh 118 lb on the ceremony Saturday. How should you respond?

options.a: Agree; event-week scale targets are standard in coaching contracts
options.b: Agree; a number guarantee is required to show you are accountable
options.c: Agree; a specific wedding-week weight is safer than a habit-focused plan
options.d: Decline; you cannot professionally guarantee a scale weight on a date

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.explanation: Body weight on one day is not fully under a coach's control (water, hormones, travel, stress). Guaranteeing 118 lb for a wedding is an outcome promise, not professional practice. Coach behaviors and a realistic timeline instead of a locked scale number.

distractorExplanations.a: Event coaching still does not make a one-day weight guarantee standard or ethical.
distractorExplanations.b: Accountability is about process and honesty, not a contractual scale promise.
distractorExplanations.c: A locked wedding weight is riskier than a habit plan because it invites crash tactics.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.prompt: A client in active chemotherapy asks you to design meals that treat the cancer and to add high-dose vitamin C. What do you do?

options.a: Refer to oncology nutrition; do not invent a cancer-treatment protocol
options.b: Write an alkaline diet because cancer is said to feed on acid
options.c: Build a ketogenic anti-cancer protocol from popular social-media posts
options.d: Prescribe megadose vitamin C as your contribution to treatment

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.explanation: Cancer treatment nutrition belongs with oncology and, often, a board-certified oncology dietitian. Coaches do not design anti-cancer meal protocols or megadose vitamin regimens. Refer, and do not compete with the medical team.

distractorExplanations.b: Alkaline diets do not treat cancer; offering one as therapy is out of scope.
distractorExplanations.c: Ketogenic cancer protocols are medical/experimental; a coach does not design them.
distractorExplanations.d: High-dose vitamin C as cancer treatment is a medical intervention, not a coaching add-on.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.prompt: A weekend 'functional blood chemistry' course advertises that PN coaches who finish it may practice medical nutrition therapy. What is true?

options.a: Finishing the course legally authorizes you to practice medical nutrition therapy
options.b: CE keeps you current; it does not grant RD licensure or MNT scope
options.c: Each certificate automatically adds a new legal scope of practice
options.d: CE replaces an ethics code, so referrals become optional afterward

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.explanation: Continuing education updates knowledge as claims and science drift. It does not turn a PN Level 1 coach into an RD or authorize medical nutrition therapy. Scope is set by law and credential, not by weekend certificates, and ethics still require referrals.

distractorExplanations.a: A CE course does not legally expand a coach into medical nutrition therapy.
distractorExplanations.c: Legal scope does not grow automatically with each certificate you collect.
distractorExplanations.d: CE complements ethics; it does not retire referral duties or an ethics code.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.prompt: Before they pay, a client asks what an informed-consent coaching agreement should actually cover. Which set belongs in it?

options.a: A waiver stating that your signature lets you give medical advice
options.b: Fees only, because nutrition coaching is unregulated in every state
options.c: What you do, what you do not do, key limits, and that they may stop
options.d: A promise of a specific number of pounds lost by week twelve

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.explanation: Informed consent describes the service, the limits (no diagnosis, no MNT, not an RD), relevant risks, and the client's right to stop. It cannot expand you into medical advice or lock a weight-loss number. Fees matter, but they are not the whole agreement.

distractorExplanations.a: Consent cannot authorize medical advice; it should state that limit, not waive it.
distractorExplanations.b: Even where coaching is lightly regulated, consent covers scope and exit rights, not only price.
distractorExplanations.d: A promised pound target is an outcome guarantee, not informed consent.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.prompt: You download another coach's paid 16-week program and drop the PDFs into a paying client's Drive folder. How should that be classified?

options.a: Fair use, provided you add a credit slide that names the original author
options.b: Acceptable, because your client already paid you for 'a program'
options.c: Allowed if you recolor the cover and rename a few of the meals
options.d: A copyright and ethics problem; you need an original coaching process

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-s.explanation: Copying an entire paid program into a client's folder is copyright infringement and an ethics failure. Credit, client payment to you, and light edits do not create a license. Build and deliver your own process.

distractorExplanations.a: Naming the author does not turn wholesale copying of a paid program into fair use.
distractorExplanations.b: Your client's fee buys your service, not another coach's copyrighted curriculum.
distractorExplanations.c: Recoloring covers and renaming meals still yields an infringing derivative work.
